Elementary Row & Column Operations
Elementary row operations on a Matrix A are defined as follows:
1 Interchanging two rows; Ri ↔ Rj
2 Multiply a row by non-zero constant c; cRi → Ri
3 Add a constant c times one row to another; cRi + Rj → Rj
Inverse elementary row operations are as follows:
1 Interchanging same two rows
2 Multiply the same row by 1/c
3 If B resulted by adding c times row Ri of A to row Rj then, add −c times Rj
to Ri
It follows that if we let B be the matrix that results from A by performing a
sequence of elementary row operations, then the matrix A can be recovered from
B by performing a second sequence of elementary row operations.
(P P Savani University) Matrix Algebra 25 / 95

Inverse of Matrix (Row operation / Gauss-Jordan Method)
Inverse of a Matrix by Gauss-Jordan Method / Elementary
Row operations
To find the inverse of an invertible matrix A, elementary row operations are performed
on A = InA to reduce the matrix A (which is on the L.H.S) to identity matrix In.
As soon as the matrix A is reduced to In then the corresponding matrix In (which is
on the R.H.S) will reduced to A−1.
This method is known as Gauss-Jordan method or Row elimination or the method
of elementary transformations.

Row Echelon Form
A given matrix A is said to be in row echelon form (REF) if
1 All zero rows of the matrix occur below the non-zero rows.
2 The first non-zero element in any non-zero row of the matrix must be equal to
1. This is called a leading 1.
3 In each non-zero column containing leading 1 all the elements below leading 1
must be equal to zero.
4 In each non-zero row the leading 1 appears below and right to the leading 1 of
the previous row.
The number of zeroes before the leading 1 in any non-zero row is less than the number
of such zeroes in the next non-zero row.

Rank of a Matrix
Properties of Rank of Matrix
1 If A is a matrix of order m × n, then ρ(A) ≤ minimum of m and n
2 If A is a square matrix of order n, then ρ(A) ≤ n
3 ρ(A) = ρ(AT ), where AT is transpose of matrix A
4 If A is a null matrix, then ρ(A) = 0
5 If A is a non-singular matrix (|A| 6 = 0) of order n, then ρ(A) = n
6 If A is a singular matrix (|A| = 0) of order n, then ρ(A) < n

System of Linear Equations Consistency of a System of Linear Equations
Consistency of a System of Linear Equations
Consistent system: The system (1) is said to be consistent if, it has atleast one
solution.
The necessary and sufficient condition that the system of linear equation AX = B is
consistent is that ρ(A) = ρ(A|B).
The system (1) may have a unique solution or infinitely many solutions.
1 If ρ(A) = ρ(A|B) = n, then there is a unique solution.
2 If ρ(A) = ρ(A|B) < n, then there are infinitely many solutions.
Inconsistent system: The system (1) is said to be inconsistent if, it has no solution.
If ρ(A) 6 = ρ(A|B) then the system is inconsistent.
To solve the system (1), use elementary row operations to convert the augmented
matrix to REF or RREF.

System of Linear Equations Consistency of a System of Linear Equations
Note: Every homogeneous system of linear equations is consistent because all such
systems have x1 = 0, x2 = 0, ..., xn = 0 as a solution. This solution is called the
trivial solution; if there are other solutions, they are called nontrivial solutions.
Because a homogeneous linear system always has the trivial solution, there are only
two possibilities for its solutions:
1 The system has only the trivial solution.
2 The system has infinitely many solutions in addition to the trivial solution.
Thus, for a homogeneous system of m linear equations in n variables if m < n, then
the system will have a non-trivial (infinitely many) solution.

Properties of Eigen Values and Eigen Vectors
1 The sum of the eigen values of a matrix is its trace (sum of its principal
diagonal elements).
2 The product of the eigen values of a matrix is the determinant (|A|) of the
matrix.
3 The eigen values of A and AT are same.
4 The eigen values of A−1 are the reciprocals of the eigen values of the eigen
values of A, i.e., if λ is an eigen value of a matrix A then 1
λ is an eigen value of
A−1.
5 The eigen values of a triangular matrix are the diagonal elements of the matrix.

Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic (eigen) equation.
i.e., If A is an n × n matrix whose characteristic equation is
λn + a1λn−1 + a2λn−2 + · · · + an = 0
then
An + a1An−1 + a2An−2 + · · · + anI = 0
Using this theorem, we can find the inverse of the given matrix.
